body:
There are questions God asks that don’t come with urgency or anger. They don’t thunder from heaven or arrive wrapped in correction. They come softly. Almost casually. Yet they linger longer than any rebuke ever could. Lately, God has been asking me one of those questions that I’ve been avoiding. Tshiamo… where are you? At first, I brushed it off. I hadn’t sinned. I hadn’t fallen away. I was still praying, still showing up, still doing what a believer is supposed to do. On the outside, everything looked fine. Productive. Even fruitful. But the question wouldn’t leave me alone. And the more I sat with it, the more I realised something unsettling: this question isn’t reserved for moments of rebellion. Sometimes God asks, “Where are you?” when nothing looks wrong at all. The first time this question appears in Scripture is in Genesis. Adam has eaten the fruit. Yes, there is sin involved, but what’s fascinating is not the failure itself. It’s God’s response. God doesn’t open with judgment. He doesn’t demand an explanation. He doesn’t even mention the sin. He simply asks, “Where are you?” God knew exactly where Adam was hiding. He knew what had been done. The question wasn’t for God’s information - it was for Adam’s awareness. God was asking Adam to locate himself. And I wonder how often God does the same with us. Adam had Eden. He had purpose. He had work to do. He had access, intimacy, authority, and vision. Everything we associate with blessing was already in his hands. Yet God still asks him, “Where are you?”\

Which tells me something important: you can be surrounded by God’s gifts and still be distant from God Himself. That thought sat heavy with me. A few mornings ago, I was on a bus heading to work. The air was cool, the birds were loud, the city was waking up. Life was moving forward as usual. My phone vibrated in my hand — a message from a friend asking for prayer. He wasn’t okay mentally. Spiritually. Physically. He said he wouldn’t be coming to church. I stared out the window for a moment before replying. The night before, I had been reading Genesis. That question had already been echoing in my spirit. And suddenly, I realised this question isn’t only asked in moments of moral failure. It’s asked in moments of quiet drifting. There are seasons when we’re not running from God we’re just floating. Still blessed. Still busy. Still involved. Still building. But no longer fully present. That’s where the danger lies. Jesus touches on this in Luke 10 through the story of Mary and Martha. Martha is busy doing everything for Jesus. She’s serving, organising, and carrying responsibility. Mary, on the other hand, is sitting. Listening. Being still. Martha isn’t wrong but she’s distracted. And Jesus gently reveals what’s missing. Mary chose intimacy. Martha chose activity. And I hear God asking again: Where are you? Not, What are you doing? Not, How much are you producing? Not, How full is your schedule? But where are you with Me?\

There’s something sobering about realising you can do many things for God while slowly stepping away from God. That you can serve Him, talk about Him, even represent Him yet neglect the place where your heart meets His. After Adam sinned, the Bible says he hid from the presence of God. But if I’m honest, we don’t always hide because of sin. Sometimes we hide because life gets loud. Because ambition gets demanding. Because responsibility consumes us. And before we realise it, intimacy becomes optional. When the church doors close on a Sunday… where are you? When the worship fades and the week begins… where are you? When the spiritual high wears off and routine takes over… where are you? This question feels like a cry in my chest. Not condemnation, invitation. God is not trying to expose us. He’s trying to draw us back. Scripture says, “Return to Me, and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7). That tells me something else: drifting is often slow, and returning is intentional. In Eden, Adam’s greatest privilege wasn’t authority or responsibility. It was fellowship. Walking with God. Hearing His voice. Being fully known without shame. And I know deep down, I can build businesses, meet deadlines, chase visions, and still lose that. There are many things this year that will try to kill intimacy. Good things, even. But none of them are worth losing the one thing that sustains a believer. So I find myself asking the question back not to God, but to myself. Tshiamo, where are you? This is a cry from me to me. A call to return. To sit again at the feet of Jesus like Mary did. To choose presence over performance. To slow down enough to be found again. Because there is nothing greater in a believer’s life than intimacy with God. Everything flows from there. Everything returns there.\

And so I ask again, not just for myself, but for the body, for the church, for anyone willing to be honest: Where are you? Not in theory. Not in appearance. But in truth. May we not be found busy but distant. May we not be found successful but lost. May we have the courage to answer honestly and the humility to return.\

**Selah**
title: Where Are You?
author: Tshiamo Ramokgadi
